lessons.title: The Building Blocks: Basic, DA, HRA, Special Allowance and Bonus

children.text: Open any payslip from Infosys, HDFC Bank or a Pune startup and you will see the same handful of lines: Basic, HRA, Special Allowance, maybe DA, maybe a bonus. They look like accounting labels. They are not. Each one is wired to something else: your PF, your gratuity, your HRA exemption, your bonus eligibility and, ultimately, your tax.
Change one line and several others move with it. This lesson shows you what each building block is, what it controls, and why HR cares so much about the size of your basic.

body.text: Basic salary is the anchor. Almost every other number on your payslip is calculated as a percentage of it.

children.text: Block 1: Basic salary, the anchor
Basic salary
is the fixed core of your pay. On its own it is simple: fully taxable, paid monthly, no exemptions. What makes it powerful is everything that is calculated from it.

markDefs.definition: The fixed core of your pay, before any allowances. It is fully taxable and is the base on which PF, gratuity, HRA and often bonus and leave encashment are calculated.

body.caption: What moves when your basic moves

cells: Your monthly deduction rises, in-hand falls
More of your CTC goes to EPF instead of cash
15/26 of monthly basic for each year of service
Capped at 40% or 50% of basic (plus DA)
Usually a number of days of basic
Each unused leave day is worth more
Usually a percentage of basic (plus DA)

children.text: Historically, Indian employers kept basic low, often 30% to 40% of CTC, and pushed the rest into allowances. Lower basic meant lower PF and gratuity costs for the company and a bigger monthly in-hand for the employee. The new Labour Codes have changed that game, which Lesson 4 of this chapter covers in detail.

body.title: The anchor test
body.question: Arjun's employer raises his basic salary but keeps his CTC exactly the same. Which of these will definitely NOT happen?
options: His employee PF deduction goes up
His monthly in-hand salary goes down
body.explanation: With CTC fixed, a higher basic also means higher employer PF and gratuity inside CTC. Something has to shrink to make room, and that is almost always special allowance, the balancing figure. So special allowance falls, it does not rise. PF deduction and gratuity go up, and in-hand typically goes down.

children.text: Block 2: Dearness Allowance, the inflation shield
Dearness Allowance (DA)

exists to protect salaries from inflation. You will see it mostly in central and state government jobs, PSUs like SBI, ONGC and Coal India, and some older manufacturing companies. Most private sector offer letters do not have it.

markDefs.definition: An allowance paid mainly to government and PSU employees to offset inflation, set as a percentage of basic pay and revised twice a year based on the consumer price index for industrial workers.

children.text: For central government employees, DA is a percentage of basic pay revised twice a year, in January and July, based on the All India Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers. From January 2026 the rate is 60% of basic.

body.caption: Central government DA, revised every January and July.

body.title: A central government salary
body.prompt: Meera joins a central government ministry at Level 7 of the 7th Pay Commission matrix with a basic pay of ₹44,900 a month. The DA rate is 60%. What is her monthly DA?
body.explanation: DA = ₹44,900 × 60% = ₹26,940 a month. Her basic plus DA is ₹71,840, and that combined figure, not basic alone, is the base for her HRA exemption cap and her retirement benefits.

body.text: DA is fully taxable. It matters for structuring because DA that forms part of retirement benefits is treated like basic for HRA exemption limits, gratuity and PF. When a rule says "basic plus DA", it is talking to government and PSU employees most of all.

children.text: Block 3: House Rent Allowance, the component with a tax door
House Rent Allowance (HRA)
is paid to help you cover rent, usually set at 40% to 50% of basic. It is the first component on this list with a genuine tax door attached.

markDefs.definition: An allowance paid to help cover rent. It is fully taxable in the new regime. In the old regime, part of it can be exempt if you actually pay rent for accommodation you live in.

body.title: HRA under the two tax regimes

columns.label: New tax regime (default)
points: Paying rent makes no difference to your tax
The HRA line is effectively just more salary

columns.label: Old tax regime
points: Part of HRA can be exempt if you pay rent and live in that home
Exemption is the least of three limits
Cap is 50% of basic plus DA in 8 cities, 40% elsewhere
Old Section 10(13A), now under Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 2025

body.label: Cities where the HRA exemption cap is 50% of basic plus DA, from tax year 2026-27
body.context: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata and Chennai, now joined by Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. All other cities remain at 40%.

children.text: The full three-way HRA calculation gets its own lesson in Chapter 2. For now, remember the structural point: a bigger basic raises both the HRA component and the maximum exemption, which is why old-regime employees paying high rent in Mumbai or Bengaluru care about basic much more than new-regime employees do.

body.title: Build the HRA line
body.prompt: Arjun's basic salary is ₹60,000 a month, and his company sets HRA at 40% of basic. What is his monthly HRA component?
body.explanation: HRA = 40% × ₹60,000 = ₹24,000 a month. Note this is the HRA component paid to him, not his exemption. Whether any of it is tax-free depends on his regime and the rent he pays.

children.text: Block 4: Special allowance, the balancing figure
Special allowance

has no legal definition and no special tax treatment. HR sets every other component first and whatever remains of the CTC is called special allowance. Some companies call it flexi allowance, supplementary allowance or other allowance. The label changes, the treatment does not: it is fully taxable.

markDefs.definition: The balancing component in a salary structure, set to whatever is left of CTC after all other components are fixed. It is fully taxable and has no linked exemption.

body.title: The one-word rule
body.textWithBlank: No matter what your employer calls it, special allowance is fully ___ under both tax regimes.
body.explanation: Special allowance has no exemption attached under either regime. Every rupee is added to your taxable salary. Specific named allowances, like certain reimbursements, can be different, and Chapter 2 covers those.

body.text: A large special allowance is a signal, not a perk. It usually means basic has been kept low, which keeps PF and gratuity low. Under the Labour Codes, allowances like this are now counted as wages for PF and gratuity purposes in many cases, so structures built on a thin basic and a fat special allowance are being redesigned across India.

children.text: Block 5: Bonus, in all its forms
Bonus is a family of payments, not one thing. What they share: every type of bonus is fully taxable as salary in the year you receive it, and your employer deducts TDS on it.

cells: Legally mandated bonus of 8.33% to 20% of wages under the Code on Wages, 2019, for employees below a government-notified wage threshold
Mostly relevant to lower-wage roles, not typical white-collar offers
Linked to your rating and company results, quoted at target in CTC
Actual payout can be well below target
One-time payment to sign, often to cover a bonus you forfeit at your old job
Clawback if you leave within 12 or 24 months
Paid for staying through a date, common in M&A and critical roles
Paid only if you are still employed on that date
Discretionary payment around Diwali or year-end
Not guaranteed and rarely in CTC

body.title: A year of bonuses for Priya, a product manager in Hyderabad

events.title: Joins with a ₹1,50,000 joining bonus
events.description: Paid in her first salary. TDS on that month jumps sharply because the full amount is taxed as salary.

events.title: Diwali ex-gratia of ₹15,000
events.description: Discretionary and outside CTC, but still fully taxable salary.

events.title: Annual variable pay at 80% of target
events.description: Target was ₹2,00,000, so she receives ₹1,60,000. Taxed in tax year 2027-28, the year it is paid.

events.title: Joining bonus clawback window ends
events.description: Her offer letter required repayment if she left within 24 months. Having crossed this date, the ₹1,50,000 is fully hers.

children.text: Same CTC, different building blocks

Now watch the blocks interact. Two employees in Pune each have a ₹15,00,000 CTC with no variable pay and no insurance. Both get HRA at 50% of basic, employer PF at 12% of basic and gratuity at 15/26 of one month's basic. The only difference is the size of basic. Both are in the new regime and pay ₹200 a month professional tax.

body.caption: Structure A (basic 30% of CTC) vs Structure B (basic 50% of CTC), annual figures

body.title: What each structure delivers per year

stats.label: Monthly in-hand, B vs A
stats.context: Structure B pays less cash every month

stats.label: Yearly retirement savings, B vs A
stats.context: More PF on both sides and higher gratuity

stats.label: Yearly income tax, B vs A
stats.context: Lower gross salary, because more CTC goes to employer PF and gratuity

body.text: Notice why Structure B pays less tax even though nothing was "exempted". Employer PF and gratuity provision sit inside CTC but outside taxable salary. The more of your CTC that flows there, the lower your gross salary and your tax. You lose about ₹78,550 of yearly in-hand but gain ₹86,423 of long-term savings, with ₹7,870 of tax saved making up the difference.

body.title: Show the working: tax under both structures

children.text: Structure A: gross ₹14,24,365 minus ₹75,000 standard deduction = taxable ₹13,49,365. Slab tax = ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + 15% of ₹1,49,365 (₹22,405) = ₹82,405. Plus 4% cess = ₹85,701, rounded to ₹85,700.
Neither gets the Section 156 rebate (Section 87A of the 1961 Act), because both taxable incomes are above ₹12,00,000.
Monthly in-hand = gross ÷ 12, minus employee PF (₹4,500 in A, ₹7,500 in B), minus ₹200 professional tax, minus tax ÷ 12.

body.title: Should Rohan push back?
body.scenario: Rohan, 27, works in Ahmedabad on a ₹15 lakh CTC with Structure A. HR announces that from next month his basic will go up to 50% of CTC, exactly like Structure B, with no change in CTC. He is in the new regime, pays ₹22,000 rent, and is saving for a flat down payment in three years. He is annoyed that his in-hand will fall by about ₹6,500 a month.
body.prompt: Is Rohan actually worse off? What should he consider before complaining to HR?
body.modelAnswer: Rohan is not poorer. His CTC is unchanged, his tax falls by ₹7,870 a year, and his yearly PF and gratuity build-up rises by ₹86,423. The real cost is liquidity: about ₹78,500 a year moves from his bank account into EPF and gratuity, which he cannot freely use for a down payment in three years. Being in the new regime, the higher basic does nothing for his HRA exemption. So the question is not "am I losing money" but "do I need this cash now". If the down payment is his priority, he can check whether EPF partial withdrawal rules for buying a house would work for him, and adjust his SIPs for the lower in-hand. Complaining to HR is unlikely to help, because the Labour Codes are pushing employers towards this kind of structure anyway.

children.text: Putting the blocks together

cards.definition: Fully taxable anchor. Drives PF, gratuity, HRA and often leave encashment and employer NPS.
Inflation-linked, mainly for government and PSU staff. Fully taxable. Often counted with basic for retirement benefits and HRA limits.
Fully taxable in the new regime. Partly exempt in the old regime if you pay rent, with a 50% cap in 8 cities and 40% elsewhere.
The balancing figure. Fully taxable under both regimes. Shrinks when basic grows.
Statutory, variable, joining, retention or festival. All fully taxable as salary in the year received.

body.title: Which block is it?
body.question: Kavya's offer letter says: "Flexi Pay: ₹4,12,800 per annum, being the residual amount of CTC after all other components." For tax purposes, what is this?
options: Part of basic, so it increases PF
A perquisite valued under separate rules
body.explanation: Whatever it is called, a residual amount of CTC with no specific purpose or proof requirement is a special allowance. It is fully taxable. It is not basic, so it does not automatically raise PF, though under the Labour Codes it may count as wages for PF and gratuity calculations.

body.text: Figures use tax year 2026-27 rules under the new tax regime unless stated. DA rates, statutory bonus thresholds and state professional tax vary and are revised periodically. This lesson is for education and is not personalised tax advice.

points: Basic salary is fully taxable, but it drives PF, gratuity, HRA, leave encashment and employer NPS limits.
DA is mostly a government and PSU component, currently 60% of basic for central government staff, and is fully taxable.
HRA is fully taxable in the new regime. In the old regime it can be partly exempt, with a 50% cap in 8 cities from tax year 2026-27.
Special allowance is the balancing figure and is always fully taxable, whatever it is called.
Every form of bonus is taxed as salary in the year it is paid.
With CTC fixed, a higher basic means lower in-hand, lower tax in the new regime and higher retirement savings.
